events.excerpt: Your tongue might not seem like the most obvious way to control a computer, but it's actually well suited to the job. It's fast, precise, and capable of reaching individual teeth without any visual guidance. Researchers at Aarhus University have taken advantage of these abilities to develop TeethMark , a wearable interface that lets users control electronic devices by touching their teeth with their tongue. The device resembles a transparent dental retainer that fits over the teeth. Embedded in the custom-made brace is a flexible printed circuit board containing electrodes that detect tongue movements through capacitive sensing. The system recognizes three types of gestures: tapping individual teeth, sliding the tongue across multiple teeth, and touching several teeth simultaneously. Unlike standard touch interfaces, TeethMark also provides electrotactile feedback. Electrodes on the inner surfaces of the teeth deliver small electrical pulses that users can feel with their tongues. Additional electrodes on the outer surfaces stimulate the inside of the lips, allowing notifications to be delivered without requiring any tongue movement. The hardware is built around an ESP32 microcontroller, which handles capacitive sensing and controls the electrical stimulation circuitry. A MOSFET
events.headline: TeethMark Puts a Computer Interface in Your Mouth

events.excerpt: As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday's global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It's not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point. It's not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus —one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever. events.excerpt: It’s the second Tuesday of the month, and that means another Microsoft Patch Tuesday. The new normal is that the numbers are hard to believe. Brian Krebs reports that this month’s release fixes nearly 1,100 vulnerabilities, 63 of them rated critical, and over 500 that let an attacker elevate their privileges. Only one is reported as actively exploited: CVE-2026-124194 , a spoofing bug in Outlook. Microsoft has now shipped more than 5,100 security fixes this year, after more than 1,400 last month, compared to an average of around 100 a month last year. Obviously AI tools get the credit for the volume of bugs fixed, but also of course for the volume of bugs found. Everyone else is busy too. Apple pushed out-of-cycle updates for at least nine vulnerabilities across its operating systems, including an iMessage flaw which could let a remote attacker join a group chat and read its messages, and backported the fixes to iOS 18. Chrome 157 fixes CVE-2026-125350 , another Chrome zero-day, a week after a Chrome release which fixed more than 200 bugs, Firefox 160 fixes almost 100 CVEs, and Adobe fixed more than 110. Also since last week, zlib 1.4 shipped with more than a dozen security fixes, eight more vulnerabilities were disclosed in the X.Org server and XWayland, and Microsoft’s own Azur

events.excerpt: Whether it's nostalgia or a sense that technology has gotten a bit too pervasive, there’s no denying that Slate Auto appears to be tuned into the particular moment. Among the things Slate does without is an embedded infotainment system. The small digital display on the dashboard that shows your speed and range is also where the backup camera appears if you engage reverse, and there are two USB-C ports that provide power but not connectivity, and that’s that. But there is a solution to getting lost, and it's called “Screenless GPS.” Even though we don’t have a Slate truck to test it with, the OEM sent us a unit to review. That’s right, it’s a good old spiral-bound road atlas! “We believe you should use the devices you know and love,” Slate says, and it reckons that maps worked just fine for past generations, so they should still work now. events.excerpt: It's a story as old as time. Billionaire nerd boy meets girl. Girl is later suspected of being a spy. News at 11. Oh, and it's also been reported that he was having an affair with one of his direct-report employees. When Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a "romantic" blunder, he doesn't do it halfway. The boss of the world's most valuable company – well, it was until recently, anyway – publicly resigned yesterday, November 12, as CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately. We don't know if he jumped or if he was pushed. He left after admitting to having an affair. Although he never named an affair partner, one of the affairs was reported to be with Alice Huang, AKA Huang Le. She's head of the Chinese company Megaspeed, which was an Nvidia partner. Megaspeed is accused of being a front for China's government that was used to transfer Nvidia chips to China, although this hasn't been proven. Some US officials also suspect [PDF] she's working for Chinese intelligence, although the DoJ said it hasn't yet reached a conclusion about this. The final nail in Jensen's coffin came when The New York Times reported he had also allegedly had an affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell. Jeeze, guy! events.excerpt: For people who are blind or visually impaired, navigating a busy city street can be difficult, even with the help of a white cane or guide dog. But what if you could sense nearby obstacles through vibrations on your skin? That's the idea behind a project by YouTuber DebackTech, who has developed an experimental pair of smart glasses that use LiDAR sensors and a vibration-equipped shirt to give wearers a sense of their surroundings without relying on sight. The plan is to give visually impaired individuals a sense of spatial awareness without resorting to cameras, audio cues, or any bulky equipment. DebackTech set out with two specific goals in mind: navigating a crowded city street without sight and catching a ball while blindfolded. The project started with a small 64-point LiDAR sensor, which measures distances by emitting light and detecting its reflections. DebackTech found that the resolution of this sensor was too low to be of much use, so he switched to a 512-point sensor and mounted three of them on a pair of glasses. An inertial measurement unit (IMU) was also added to track head movements and orientation. Climate Action Tracker , a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5° Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement . When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7° Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. Compatibility Mode lets a newer version of Word open a document created in an older version, such as Word 2010, without changing its layout.
